target: Il y habite depuis trois ans.
english: He has lived there for three years.
tip: 'Y' replaces location: 'il y habite' = he lives there. Position: before the conjugated verb.

target: Tu pars pour combien de temps ?
english: How long are you leaving for?
tip: 'pour' marks a planned stretch of time, not time already spent: 'pour combien de temps' = for how long you'll be gone. Elapsed time takes 'pendant'.

target: Il a envoyé le rapport par courriel.
english: He sent the report by email.
tip: Par marks the means or channel, like English 'by' or 'via': par courriel = by email. Same in par téléphone, par la poste.

target: Elle les a lus en une semaine.
english: She read them in one week.
tip: Slip a direct object before avoir and the past participle agrees: les a lus grows an s. Drop the les and it stays lu.

target: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
english: I would like a coffee, please.
tip: "Voudrais" is the conditional of vouloir. Used for polite requests.

target: Mon père veut que j'aille à l'université.
english: My father wants me to go to university.
tip: English says 'wants me to go', but French won't cross two subjects with a plain infinitive: veut que j'aille (from aller), subjunctive.

target: Elle a peur que ses enfants soient malades.
english: She's afraid her children are sick.
tip: "Avoir peur que" expresses fear and triggers the subjunctive.

target: Il est surprenant que personne n'ait remarqué l'erreur.
english: It's surprising that no one noticed the mistake.
tip: Surprise about something already done takes the past subjunctive: que personne n'ait remarqué – ait, not the everyday 'a'.

target: Je ne suis pas sûr que tu aies raison.
tip: You aren't right in French, you HAVE reason: avoir raison. Being right always uses a form of avoir – tu aies raison here.

target: Si nous avions plus d'argent, nous achèterions une maison.
english: If we had more money, we would buy a house.
tip: Si + imparfait, conditionnel: si nous avions → nous achèterions. Never use conditional after si.

target: Nous en avons acheté deux kilos.
english: We bought two kilos of it.
tip: En replaces the noun after a quantity: deux kilos de pommes becomes en... deux kilos.

target: Nous partirons à moins qu'il neige.
tip: "À moins que" (unless) requires the subjunctive.
English wastes 'water' with no article, but French needs the partitive: gaspille de l'eau = wastes some water. Uncountable things always take du, de la or de l'.
You don't trust someone directly in French – you 'make trust TO' them: faire confiance à. So it's lui, not le: Je lui fais confiance.
When two pronouns stack, me/te/nous come before le/la/les: te le, not le te. Je te le promets = I promise it to you, the reverse of English word order.
In a negative command the pronoun stays BEFORE the verb: Ne lui dis rien. Only positive commands push it after, as in dis-lui.
En avoir entendu parler = to have heard about it. En replaces de + topic.
réfléchir à quelque chose = think about it. The à-phrase collapses to y, sitting before the verb: il y réfléchit = he's thinking about it.
en avoir marre = to be fed up. The en is baked into the idiom and can't be dropped: Nous en avons marre = we've had enough.
manquer flips the subject: Il me manque = I miss him, literally 'he is lacking to me'. The person missed is the subject; the one missing them is me/te/lui.
devoir means both 'must' and 'owe'. Here it's owe, and you owe TO someone: Nous lui devons beaucoup = we owe him a lot. So lui, not le.

english: Talk to them about your project.
tip: In a positive command the pronoun hooks onto the verb with a hyphen: parle-leur = talk to them. parler à quelqu'un takes leur, not les.
répondre à quelqu'un = answer someone. French answers TO a person, so the pronoun is lui, not le: Tu lui as répondu?
Se souvenir de becomes s'en souvenir. The reflexive and en both go before the verb.
Short adverbs like déjà slip between the two parts of the past tense: avons déjà réservé, not 'avons réservé déjà'. English keeps 'already' outside.
dépendre uses de where English uses 'on': Je dépends de mes parents = I depend ON my parents. The preposition rarely matches English.
Double pronouns: les (direct) + leur (indirect). Les goes before leur.
After a preposition French switches to stressed pronouns: avec moi, not 'avec je'. Same with toi, lui, eux: Je la prends avec moi.
à emporter = to take away, to go. It's the standard phrase for takeaway food: le prenons à emporter = we're getting it to go.
A reflexive verb in a positive command swaps te for toi and attaches it: habille-toi = get dressed. Only positive commands make this switch.
